chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan, from al-Husayn (his brother), from his father Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Abu al-Hasan (the preceding Imam), peace be upon him, who said:

I asked him about drinking the fermented drink (fuqa') that is made in the market and sold, and I do not know how it was made or when it was made. He said: 'Is it permissible for me to drink it?' He replied, 'I do not like it.'

key_terms.أَحِلُّ: Permissible or lawful, referring to the legal status of the drink.
key_terms.السُّوقِ: The market, referring to the place of trade and sale.
key_terms.الْفُقَّاعُ: A fermented drink, often made from dates or grapes, common in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabia.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on drinking fermented beverages sold in the market when their preparation method is unknown?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) responded to a query about 'fuqa'' (a common fermented drink) sold in markets with uncertain preparation methods by stating 'I do not like it' (la uhibbuhu). In Shia jurisprudence, this phrase often signifies 'makruh' (disliked) or a mild prohibition, reflecting the principle of 'istishab' (presumption of continuity) where the default state of such beverages is considered impure or mixed with unknown elements until proven otherwise. This highlights the scholarly emphasis on caution (ihtiyat) in consumables where the chain of custody and processing details are obscured.
